stops.name: Córdoba, the new fashion of the hair
stops.campa: He remakes how Córdoba wears its hair and its face besides: a short, banged style that leaves the neck, the ears, and the eyebrows bare, replacing the long, ear-covering braids women have worn for generations; close shaving for the men who follow the court's lead; new depilatory pastes, shaped eyebrows, scented oils worked through the hair in place of plain rosewater. What begins as the emir's own household style spreads outward through the merchant class, then further, until Córdoba's streets themselves look visibly different from what they looked like a decade before.

stops.name: Córdoba, tooth-powder and the morning bath
stops.campa: Among the smaller reforms that outlast him: a dentifrice of his own recipe, described as both effective and pleasant to the taste, and a preparation against the odor of the body, urged on the court alongside a discipline of washing morning and evening that many Córdobans have not troubled with before. It is easy, from a great distance, to laugh at hygiene as a legacy; it is harder to find another single figure credited with moving an entire city's daily habit of the body, and Andalusi writers a century later still trace the custom back to him by name.

stops.name: Córdoba, the table remade
stops.campa: At the emir's table Ziryab replaces the old custom of setting everything out on one broad platter with a sequence of his own design: soup first, then meat or fowl or fish, then fruit and sweets and nuts to close the meal, each course cleared before the next arrives, all of it laid on fine leather rather than bare wood. He is credited too with putting asparagus on Andalusi tables for the first time, and with replacing the court's heavy metal drinking vessels with crystal, so the wine, or in devout households the sherbet, can be seen as well as tasted.

stops.name: Córdoba, chess, polo, and the astrologers from India
stops.campa: Ziryab's curiosity runs well past music and manners. He brings word and practice of games newly fashionable at Baghdad — chess foremost among them, and a form of polo — into the Córdoban court's leisure, and is said to have encouraged the arrival of astrologers out of India, carrying methods of reading the stars the Umayyad court had not seen before. Little of this survives as clearly attributed fact the way the oud or the nawbat do, but the pattern holds: whatever the wider Abbasid world knows, Córdoba, through Ziryab, comes to know shortly after.

stops.name: Córdoba, the Mezquita rising alongside him
stops.campa: Through these same years Abd al-Rahman II enlarges the Great Mosque of Córdoba, extending Abd al-Rahman I's original hall further south with new bays of the same red-and-white striped arches, a building program running in parallel with everything Ziryab is doing to the emirate's taste in music, dress, and food. Patron and nadim are remaking Córdoba together, one in stone and one in habit, and the city that results — mosque, table, wardrobe, and song reorganized within a single generation — will be remembered as the moment Córdoba stopped imitating Baghdad and became a capital in its own right.

stops.name: Córdoba, the taste that outran the court
stops.campa: What begins inside the palace does not stay there. Merchants who supply the emir's household adopt his fashions to sell them; the upper classes of the city copy the court that copies Ziryab; and in time, so the Andalusi chroniclers claim, something of it passes even to Córdoba's Christian and Jewish neighbors, and outward again along the trade roads into the rest of Europe — the seasonal wardrobe, the ordered courses of a formal meal, the crystal glass, habits so thoroughly absorbed within a few centuries that no one drinking from a stemmed glass in Paris or Toledo will remember where the custom started.

stops.name: Córdoba, the house of eight sons and two daughters
stops.campa: Ziryab's own household becomes, in effect, the second generation of his school. His son Ubayd Allah grows into the most celebrated singer of the family after his father; his daughter Hamduna, trained alongside her brothers, marries into the vizierate; another daughter, Ulaiya, absorbs more of his personal repertoire and his surviving students than any of her siblings. Five of the eight sons and both daughters build careers as musicians in their own right, so that by Ziryab's later years half the notable voices of Córdoba trace their training to one house on one street.

stops.name: Córdoba, thirty years the emir's companion
stops.campa: Nearly three decades on from the audience that made him nadim, Ziryab is still at Abd al-Rahman II's side, an old man now by the standards of the age, his hair gone from the black of a Baghdad prodigy to the grey of a Córdoban institution. The arrangement between them, once a gamble on a stranded refugee, has become the single fact every visiting embassy is told about the Umayyad court: that its emir keeps at his table the greatest musician the western world has produced, and pays him like it.

stops.name: Córdoba, the death of the emir
stops.campa: Abd al-Rahman II dies in the year 852, after thirty years on the Córdoban throne, and the court Ziryab did so much to shape passes to his son Muhammad I. The new emir has grown up inside the world Ziryab built — the music, the table, the dress — and continues the patronage more or less unbroken, but something of the original partnership, the two men near in age who remade a capital together, cannot be renewed with a different sovereign. Ziryab, past sixty now, keeps his school, his salary, and his household, and outlives his great patron by five years.

stops.name: Córdoba, the death of Ziryab
stops.campa: Ziryab dies in Córdoba in the year 857, in the city he reached as a penniless exile thirty-five years before and leaves as the founder of its music, its table, and half its manners. Al-Maqqari, writing centuries afterward but drawing on the Córdoban record, sums up what the whole tradition agrees on beneath its disagreements over dates and anecdotes: that there was never, before him or after him, a man of his profession more generally beloved and admired. He is buried in the city that paid him like a prince for the privilege of being remade by him.
stops.quote: There never was, either before or after him, a man of his profession who was more generally beloved and admired.

stops.name: Tétouan, the Kunnash al-Ha'ik gathers what remains
stops.campa: Nine and a half centuries after Ziryab shapes his twenty-four nawbat, one for each hour, the Moroccan poet and musician Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Ha'ik sits in Tétouan and gathers into a single songbook, the Kunnash, whatever of that vast structure still survives in living memory: eleven nawbat of the original twenty-four, their poems and their modal architecture fixed at last in writing after a thousand years of mouth-to-ear transmission. What Ziryab began as a courtier's private repertoire in Córdoba becomes, through al-Ha'ik's book, the fixed canon still performed today by the Andalusi orchestras of Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya — the blackbird's furthest and longest-carrying song.
